title: Backward-loop cast-on
subtitle: The fastest cast-on for adding a small number of stitches mid-row.
excerpt: The backward-loop cast-on wraps the working yarn around the thumb and slips the loop onto the needle. One move per stitch. Useful for a handful of mid-row additions but unstable for large cast-ons.
sourceNotes: Mary Thomas's Knitting Book (1938). One of the oldest documented cast-on methods in Beeton's Book of Needlework (1870).

glossaryTerms.definition: The simplest cast-on method: a loop of working yarn is twisted over the thumb and slipped onto the needle. Fast but unstable for more than a few stitches.

content.text: is the fastest possible way to put a stitch on the needle: loop the working yarn over the left thumb, rotate the thumb upward, and slip the loop onto the right needle. One move, one stitch. The resulting loops are unstable and collapse the moment they are worked into, which is why this method is only reliable for casting on two to five stitches mid-row, such as completing a buttonhole after casting off. For a starting edge, the long-tail or cable cast-on is more reliable. Difficulty: beginner.
Working yarn already attached (mid-row use case)
Hold the working yarn in the right hand or drape it over the left index finger.
Insert the left thumb under the yarn from below and rotate it upward, forming a loop.
Insert the needle tip into the front of the thumb loop, from left to right.
Slip the loop off the thumb onto the needle and tug the yarn lightly to close the stitch.
Repeat for the required number of stitches, then continue knitting across the row.

Patterns call for the backward-loop cast-on at the end of a buttonhole row ('cast on 3 stitches') and at the tops of sock toes where a small number of stitches bridges the gap. It is also used by teachers showing the absolute minimum required to put yarn on a needle, because the motion is intuitive and no tail is required. For any cast-on of more than 10 stitches, choose a different method.

items.symptom: Stitches autumn off the needle before they are worked
items.fix: Close each loop firmly after placing it on the needle. Consider using the cable cast-on for buttonholes if the loops keep dropping.

items.symptom: Large cast-on edge looks loose and uneven
items.cause: The backward-loop method is inherently unstable at scale
items.fix: Use this method for 5 stitches or fewer. For a full edge, use the long-tail or cable cast-on.
